attribution: Traditionally attributed to Shankara, with some verses ascribed by tradition to his disciples; authorship debated
summary: A popular devotional hymn, also called Moha Mudgara ('hammer of delusion'), urging the listener to turn from worldly preoccupations to God.
whyRead: Short, rhythmic and widely sung, it blends Advaita's call to dispassion with devotion to Govinda (Krishna). It shows that Advaita as lived is not only intellectual.
story: According to a well-known tradition, Shankara composed the refrain on seeing an old scholar in Varanasi memorising grammar rules, and his disciples added further verses; the story is traditional rather than historical.
questions: Why do we postpone what matters most?
What use is learning if it does not free us?

keyTeachings.title: Impermanence of worldly goals
keyTeachings.text: The verses point to the passing of youth, wealth and relationships to shake the listener out of complacency.

keyTeachings.title: Learning is not enough
keyTeachings.text: Mere scholarly skill, the hymn suggests, will not help at the hour of death.

keyTeachings.title: Turn to God
keyTeachings.text: Its refrain calls the listener to worship Govinda, joining dispassion with devotion.
